articles.title: When the Saudi desert was green: A 125,000-year-old lakeside reveals how early humans lived
articles.dek: Megafauna remains, stone tools and rare plant material recovered from the 125,000-year-old lakeside site of Uruq al-Julaybah in Mundafan, southern Saudi Arabia, provide one…
paragraphs: Megafauna remains, stone tools and rare plant material recovered from the 125,000-year-old lakeside site of Uruq al-Julaybah in Mundafan, southern Saudi Arabia, provide one of the most detailed pictures yet of prehistoric human life in Arabia. Together, the discoveries reveal how early people lived, hunted and used their environment during a greener, wetter period in Arabian history.

Published in Science , the study brings together King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) researchers spanning geology, archaeology, botany and micropaleontology alongside colleagues at Griffith University and the Saudi Heritage Commission and several other international institutions. The findings add significant evidence to Saudi Arabia's deep human and environmental history and contribute to a wider understanding of early human presence across the Arabian Peninsula.

Researchers used satellite terrain modeling to map the approximately 340 km² (131 square miles) ancient lake, which reached a maximum depth of 29 meters (95 feet). Sediments, geomorphological data and aquatic remains indicated a relatively stable freshwater body surrounded by vegetation and open grasslands.

The team also carried out systematic grid surveys to collect fossils and stone tools, used two dating methods on sand and fossil teeth, applied 3D-refitting techniques to stone tools, and conducted microscopic and chemical residue analysis of tool surfaces. This comprehensive methodology provided direct insights into how early human populations lived and adapted during the last interglacial period , a warm, humid phase approximately 125,000 years ago commonly known as Green Arabia.

The team documented more than 500 fossil specimens of plants and animals, including invertebrates, at more than 130 locations across the site. Animal remains included hippos, extinct long-horned buffaloes, camels, Arabian oryx, gazelles and ostriches.

Researchers collected 5,511 stone tools larger than 2 cm (0. 8 inches) from the main study area. More than 98% were made of flint, and analyses showed the use of Levallois techniques in stone tool production.

The tools contain residues of a wide variety of plants, including some that are toxic. Traces of resin and woody tissue suggest the use of hafted weapon tips, while plant residues indicate the processing of tubers, bushes and palm leaves. These traces point to varied uses of plants for food and everyday tasks.

Among the most significant findings is evidence of the potential use of toxic plant compounds in hunting technology, understood to be among the first examples of such evidence recorded in Saudi Arabia, alongside some of the earliest evidence of palm-related vegetation found in the region. Together, these findings paint a picture of a population making diverse and sophisticated use of their environment.

What makes this site exceptional is that all of these elements (animal remains, stone tools and plant material) were found together in a single, dated context, allowing researchers to reconstruct in unusual detail the daily lives of the people who occupied this lakeside. The site provides a vivid and unusually complete picture of how humans lived in Green Arabia.

The findings also indicate that the shores of ancient Lake Mundafan brought together freshwater, animals, plants and raw materials during the humid period around 125,000 years ago. This combination supported a range of human activities, including stone tool production, the preparation of hunting equipment, the processing of animal and plant resources, and fiber working.

"It is very exciting to see how the collaboration of so many different specialists allows us to reconstruct this uniquely complete picture of life, behavior and the environment in the distant past," said professor Frans van Buchem, KAUST professor of geology and co-lead scientist.

Dr. Faisal Al-Jibreen, a participating researcher from the Heritage Commission and a professor of Paleolithic archaeology, described the discovery in the sands of Lake Mundafan in the Empty Quarter as an important archaeological find that sheds light on the ancient environment and its relationship with humans and animals in southern Saudi Arabia's early prehistory.

articles.title: Alzheimer’s Breakthrough Reveals What Happens When the Brain’s Cleaning System Fails
articles.dek: A new study suggests that a little-understood genetic risk factor may influence Alzheimer’s progression by weakening the brain’s natural defenses against toxic plaques.
paragraphs: A new study suggests that a little-understood genetic risk factor may influence Alzheimer’s progression by weakening the brain’s natural defenses against toxic plaques.

A gene linked to Alzheimer’s disease may play a crucial role in protecting the brain from toxic protein buildup. Researchers at UVA Health have discovered that CASS4 helps immune cells contain harmful plaques, and experiments in mice show that disrupting the gene can accelerate plaque accumulation, damage neurons, and contribute to cognitive decline.

The findings suggest that CASS4 influences Alzheimer’s primarily through the brain’s immune system rather than by acting directly in nerve cells, as some scientists previously suspected. Researchers now believe that restoring or strengthening its activity could offer a new approach to treating the disease.

Alzheimer’s disease, which affects more than 6 million Americans, is characterized by the accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques and abnormal tangles of tau proteins in the brain. These changes are associated with progressive damage to neurons and worsening memory and cognitive function.

Specialized immune cells called microglia help defend the brain against these threats. When functioning properly, they gather around amyloid-beta plaques, form protective barriers, and compress the deposits into smaller, more compact structures that can limit their harmful effects.

Researchers led by John Lukens, PhD, found that CASS4 plays an important role in this protective process. In laboratory mice lacking normal CASS4 function, microglia became less effective at surrounding and compacting plaques. Amyloid deposits accumulated more aggressively, neuronal damage increased, and the animals experienced cognitive decline.

Although previous genetic studies had repeatedly associated CASS4 with Alzheimer’s risk, scientists had little understanding of its biological function. The UVA team investigated how the gene influences microglial activity and what happens when that activity is disrupted.

“Despite CASS4 being an Alzheimer’s risk gene, really nothing is known about what this gene does or how it affects the brain during disease. Our lab sought to address this major knowledge gap with this paper,” said Addie Walsh, a UVA physiology graduate student and the study’s first author. “These are important findings because they give us new insight into how this understudied AD risk gene functions in the brain and suggest that CASS4 may normally help microglia respond to amyloid pathology.”

Disrupting CASS4 also triggered widespread changes in gene activity. The researchers suspect that some of these alterations could be relevant to other neurodegenerative disorders, although the gene’s involvement in those conditions remains under investigation.

The results raise the possibility that CASS4 could eventually help researchers identify Alzheimer’s related changes earlier or develop therapies that improve the brain’s ability to manage amyloid plaques. However, the findings come from preclinical research, and further studies are needed to determine whether targeting the gene would benefit patients.

“These findings break new ground in our understanding of how this genetic risk factor contributes to Alzheimer’s disease,” said Lukens, director of UVA’s Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer’s and Neurodegenerative Diseases. “Our work further suggests that defective CASS4 activity may serve as an early-onset biomarker to detect Alzheimer’s and that therapeutic strategies which boost its function may offer a much-needed approach to treat this devastating brain disease.”

The study also supports growing research into how immune dysfunction contributes to neurodegeneration. Rather than focusing exclusively on neurons or the proteins that accumulate around them, scientists are increasingly investigating whether modifying microglial responses could help protect brain tissue.

“We are now actively exploring potential roles for CASS4 in multiple other neurodegenerative disorders and developing novel strategies to therapeutically target it,” said Lukens, of the Department of Neuroscience at the University of Virginia School of Medicine. “Many in the field initially presumed that CASS4 was likely functioning in neurons to influence Alzheimer’s. Our findings shift this paradigm by proving that CASS4 predominantly acts through the immune system. This is particularly exciting, as it has only been in recent years that immune-targeting strategies have been considered for the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases, and this remains an untapped therapeutic avenue with tremendous potential.”
Walsh plans to continue investigating the role of microglia in neurodegenerative diseases as she moves into pharmaceutical research.

articles.title: Dark matter–hunting satellite Euclid reveals record number of cosmic 'magnifying glasses'
articles.dek: UBC researchers have helped uncover 15,000 new potential strong gravitational lenses—the largest collection of these cosmic tools that help astronomers investigate dark matter.
paragraphs: UBC researchers have helped uncover 15,000 new potential strong gravitational lenses—the largest collection of these cosmic tools that help astronomers investigate dark matter.

The first major release of data from the European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope comprises 1. 7 million gigabytes of data. Analysis by a global consortium of more than 2,000 scientists, including more than 30 Canadians, revealed more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million quasars—the brilliant cores of distant galaxies—across almost 5% of the entire night sky from 13 months of observation.

"Strong lenses have been difficult to find—the odds were about 1 in 10,000," said co-author Hrishabh Srivastava, a doctoral student in the UBC department of physics and astronomy (PHAS). "Before Euclid, we had fewer than 1,000 confirmed strong lenses. Now we have 15,000 new candidates."

The Euclid satellite launched in 2023 at a cost of more than $1 billion with the aim of mapping more than one-third of the sky to build a 3D map of the universe, which would help scientists determine the properties of dark energy and dark matter on a universal scale.

Dark energy and dark matter remain two of the greatest mysteries of modern physics despite making up about 95% of the universe. Dark energy is an unknown force pushing the universe apart and observed only by the accelerating expansion of galactic objects away from each other in all directions.
Dark matter is some form of invisible, unknown matter that we can only detect through its gravitational effects—including the bending or "lensing" of light.

"It turns out, the stuff humans are made of is relatively rare in the universe," said co-author Dr. Douglas Scott, PHAS professor and a member of the Euclid collaboration. "And what dominates—dark matter and dark energy—is invisible so we're not used to dealing with it. But it makes the universe what it is; it drives how the universe expands and what the past and future of the universe will be. Where did these things come from? What properties do they have? Euclid's data give us the potential to answer those questions."

Canadian organizations involved in the Euclid mission include UBC, University of Waterloo, NRC's Herzberg Astronomy and Astrophysics Research Center, the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope and many others.

Gravitational lensing occurs when the light from one galaxy is bent by a foreground galaxy acting as a lens. The light from the more distant galaxy appears, in a perfect example, as a ring of light around the foreground galaxy, known as an Einstein ring thanks to his prediction of the phenomenon back in 1936. The composition and distribution of matter in the foreground, including dark matter, are revealed by how the light is bent.
"I like to call these gravitational lenses 'nature's own magnifying glasses' to probe the dark matter distribution of our universe," said Srivastava.
"It took many decades to verify Einstein's prediction of gravitational lenses, but if he had the Euclid data it would have been easy to confirm, since they're all over the sky," added Scott.

Gravitational lenses can also be used to investigate dark energy by plugging their parameters into the current cosmological model and seeing if the numbers match. They also magnify the background galaxy for a clearer picture.

Srivastava was part of the team finding gravitational lens candidates. This four-part process involves machine learning to initially parse the huge amount of data for likely lenses. Then, thousands of citizen scientists pore over the AI-sorted data to further refine the candidate pool. Third, experts including Srivastava check the citizen scientists' work, looking at about 6,000 to 10,000 galaxies each. The final step involves verifying that the candidates are indeed lenses using follow-up data with other telescopes.

The new catalog is larger than all previous collections of strong gravitational lenses combined. Because the observations were gathered by the same telescope and analyzed using the same methods, researchers can compare them more reliably than ever before.

articles.title: A Massive Search of 24,000 Crystals Reveals Thousands of New Possibilities
articles.dek: A computer search has identified thousands of crystals worth testing as sources of ultrathin materials, potentially widening the options for future electronics.
paragraphs: A computer search has identified thousands of crystals worth testing as sources of ultrathin materials, potentially widening the options for future electronics.

Peel a crystal down to a sheet just a few atoms thick, and you may change what the material can do. Its electrical, magnetic, or chemical behavior can shift, opening possibilities for electronics, energy storage, and faster chemical reactions.
These ultrathin sheets are known as two-dimensional, or 2D, materials. They have attracted scientific and technological interest since graphene was produced in 2004.

The challenge is finding crystals that will yield a sheet that holds together. Researchers have mostly started with crystals built like books, whose layers peel apart relatively easily because weak forces hold them together. Crystals with strong bonds running in every direction are much harder to separate.

A team at the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR) and TU Dresden has now developed the first efficient computational method for predicting separable atomic layers in any type of crystal. The findings, published in Nature Communications , give researchers a much wider selection of materials to investigate.

The team screened more than 24,000 known, non-layered crystal structures from one of the largest experimental materials databases and selected 2,531 particularly promising candidates for detailed calculations. These candidates would retain their chemical composition when a layer separated, and their calculated bonding ratios strongly favored a two-dimensional structure.

The predicted sheets differed markedly from existing database entries. Some could become metallic even though their original crystals are semiconductors, a fundamental change in how they carry electricity. Others could develop a direct band gap, an electronic feature potentially useful for devices that absorb or emit light. Magnetic candidates could also support spintronics, which uses electron spin to process and store data.

For most candidates, calculations indicated that separating a layer would require comparatively little energy. Many also appeared stable against small atomic disturbances and energetically favorable, basic requirements for technological use. Experiments must establish whether these materials can actually be made and under what conditions.

“Given that this class of materials is still so young, selecting suitable materials for experiments was often based on experience and intuition,” explains Dr. Rico Friedrich of HZDR’s Institute of Ion Beam Physics and Materials Research and TU Dresden. “Using our universal method, we can now determine the points at which a crystal in any material can best be split and whether a potentially stable two-dimensional structure can form in the process.”

The method starts by calculating how strongly individual atoms are bonded. Its core model, called the eXfoliation and Cleavage Potential, or XCP, makes these precise calculations using the elements involved and the distances between atoms.

Two additional algorithms then look for ways to separate a sheet. One searches for easily separable planes within the crystal. The other gradually removes the weakest bonds from the model until two-dimensional structures remain. The approach also detects separation surfaces that are uneven at the atomic scale.

“Calculating the electronic structure for every conceivable surface would be incredibly time-consuming,” says lead author Tom Barnowsky. “Our efficient model, on the other hand, can search big materials databases with minimal computational effort. Detailed calculations are only required for particularly promising hits.”

Tests across a wide range of two-dimensional materials already produced experimentally showed that XCP reliably identified the preferred planes for separating layers. The method is freely available as a web tool .

“Our results vastly expand the horizon for two-dimensional materials,” says Friedrich. “The method doesn’t guarantee that every candidate can be produced in the lab. But it does show which crystals are actually worth the experimental effort.”

articles.title: The experiments improving our understanding of volcanic tsunamis
articles.dek: Tsunamis triggered by volcanic eruptions are poorly understood because of the complex dynamics governing how falling rocks and ash interact with seawater to generate waves.
paragraphs: Tsunamis triggered by volcanic eruptions are poorly understood because of the complex dynamics governing how falling rocks and ash interact with seawater to generate waves. As a result, it is difficult to anticipate whether a volcanic flow will trigger a tsunami and, if so, how big it will be. Researchers have used laboratory experiments to study this process, but little is known about how well these models mimic reality.

In their article published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Oceans , A. Bougouin and colleagues addressed these uncertainties by comparing results from lab experiments to observations from a real volcano: Stromboli Island, Italy. Why Stromboli? The volcano erupts nearly constantly, and volcanic flows frequently enter the sea and form tsunamis. These events are recorded by a unique monitoring system made up of land-based cameras and offshore wave gauges—making Stromboli a sort of laboratory in the field.

The researchers focused on three Stromboli eruptions that triggered tsunamis between 2019 and 2021, comparing observations from Stromboli with results from both existing and newly conducted laboratory experiments.

In the lab, the team used a 7-meter-long, 20-centimeter-wide channel filled with water. They then released a mass of polystyrene beads (small spheres used in applications such as beanbag filling and product packaging) down a slope designed to replicate Stromboli's flank, sending the beads tumbling into the water. These lightweight beads were used to represent Stromboli's pyroclastic flows because the flows were expected to be predominantly less dense than water. Despite their buoyancy, these flows can still generate substantial waves.

The researchers found that lab experiments cannot be directly scaled up to predict real-world events and that most models based on these experiments overestimate the size of tsunamis in the field. The new experiments, however, helped bridge this gap, although some limitations remain. They reproduced key features observed at Stromboli, including a three-wave pattern, and broadly captured the energy transfer from the flow to the resulting wave train.
Researchers conducted the first direct comparison between lab experiments and field observations, providing an initial step toward improving volcanic tsunami hazard assessment.

articles.title: Scientists Uncover a Bizarre Quantum Effect Where Time Could Flow at Different Speeds Simultaneously
articles.dek: Scientists have developed a theoretical framework that could allow atomic clocks to reveal a strange quantum effect in which different flows of time exist simultaneously.
paragraphs: Scientists have developed a theoretical framework that could allow atomic clocks to reveal a strange quantum effect in which different flows of time exist simultaneously.

Raise an atomic clock by just a few millimeters, and it ticks slightly faster because gravity is weaker at the higher position. Today’s most precise clocks can detect this tiny difference, confirming a prediction of Einstein’s theory of relativity. But quantum physics introduces a stranger possibility: A single clock could exist in a superposition of different motions, potentially experiencing multiple rates of time simultaneously.

Scientists have now developed a theoretical method to detect the quantum effects of these different flows of time using advanced atomic clocks. Published in Physical Review Letters , the research shows how trapped-ion clocks could reveal a previously unobserved connection between quantum mechanics and relativity. The proposed approach uses existing experimental technology and could bring researchers closer to testing how time behaves in the quantum world.

According to Einstein’s theory of relativity, time passes at different rates depending on an object’s speed and the strength of gravity. Atomic clocks are sensitive enough to detect these differences across height changes of just a few millimeters. They measure time using precise atomic frequencies and are essential to technologies such as GPS.

Quantum mechanics introduces another possibility. An atomic clock’s motion can exist in a superposition of different states, potentially exposing it to multiple rates of time simultaneously. Under these conditions, the clock’s motion becomes entangled with its internal energy, producing changes in its quantum properties that researchers believe can be measured.

“It’s the precision that led us to develop our theoretical model. We found that the atomic clock’s motion becomes “entangled” with its internal energy. The signature of this entanglement is that the clock itself loses some of its quantum properties, which can be detected using modern techniques,” explains Associate Professor Joshua Foo of Kyushu University’s Institute for Advanced Studies, one of the study’s lead authors.

The international research team, led by scientists at Kyushu University and working with collaborators in the United States, Canada, and Sweden, also developed a theoretical approach for precisely controlling the motion of trapped ions. This could substantially increase the detectability of the quantum effect.
“We introduced a new technique for controlling the atomic clock’s motion, improving its sensitivity to this effect by 100 to 1000 times.”

The next challenge is to translate the theoretical framework into an experiment that can reliably detect the predicted quantum signature while accounting for disturbances and uncertainties in real laboratory conditions. If successful, the approach could establish atomic clocks as tools for investigating the quantum behavior of time and potentially improve future clock technology.

“Naturally, bringing our theoretical model to reality is the big next step, and developing a detailed experiment that accounts for real-world unpredictability will give us further insight into our model,” concludes Foo. “We are also interested in exploring whether atomic clocks could eventually be used to probe the quantum realm of gravity, the other fundamental question in physics.”

articles.title: James Webb Telescope Reveals a Giant Planet That Was Hiding in Plain Sight
articles.dek: Finding planets like Earth may depend on better ways to read telescope images, after a new technique uncovered a giant world already captured by JWST.
paragraphs: Finding planets like Earth may depend on better ways to read telescope images, after a new technique uncovered a giant world already captured by JWST.

A giant planet was hiding in observations taken by NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), even though astronomers already knew it existed. The telescope had captured its faint light, but the overwhelming glow of its host star made the planet impossible to distinguish using conventional image-processing techniques.

This is one of the biggest challenges in photographing planets beyond our solar system. Stars are extraordinarily bright compared with the worlds orbiting them, and even JWST, which can observe galaxies billions of years in the past, struggles to separate a planet’s faint signal from its star’s glare.

Researchers led by Northwestern University developed a new computational technique that helped overcome this problem. By accounting for tiny imperfections in the telescope, they improved its sensitivity to faint planets by 2 to 15 times and recovered a giant planet that had remained hidden in two-year-old observations. Their findings were published in the journal Nature .

“Planets are a million times fainter than their stars,” said Northwestern’s Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, who led the study. “So, to image exoplanets, we need to remove that glare. That is a very tricky problem because even the tiniest changes in the telescope can affect how that glare appears. Slight shifts or tilts — even on the scale of just a few nanometers — can change the pattern of light. Our method models how light travels through the telescope and accounts for those tiny changes, allowing us to remove the glare much more precisely.”

Ferrer-Chavez is a Ph. D. student in astronomy at Northwestern’s Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences and a member of Jason Wang’s research group. Wang, an assistant professor of physics and astronomy at Weinberg, co-authored the study. Both researchers belong to Northwestern’s Center for Interdisciplinary Exploration and Research in Astrophysics (CIERA).

Astronomers have long relied on specialized instruments called coronagraphs to block starlight when searching for planets. Even relatively bright young giant planets can be 100,000 times fainter than their stars, making this step essential. However, some light still escapes around the coronagraph, creating patterns of glare that can conceal nearby objects.

“For the past 20 years, astronomers have tackled this problem by observing a different star and using its image as a reference,” Wang said. “Then, they subtract that reference image from the original observation to remove the unwanted glare to reveal faint planets that otherwise might be hidden.”

The difficulty is that a telescope never remains perfectly still. Minute changes in its mirrors and other components can alter how starlight spreads across an image. Even a slight mismatch between the reference photograph and the original observation can leave enough residual glare to hide a planet.

“We try to make telescopes extremely stable, but there are extreme engineering challenges that we haven’t quite solved yet,” Wang said. “There are known causes of instability and unknown causes. Small thermal changes could cause a mirror to expand or contract by a picometer. Telescopes like JWST have cryocoolers to keep the instrument super cold. Those coolers have little motors that can cause the mirrors to vibrate. So, there are issues like those but also issues that we still don’t understand as we learn how to build these complex telescopes.”

To address these limitations, the Northwestern researchers developed Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP). Instead of relying entirely on reference photographs, the technique creates a digital twin of the telescope, a computer model that recreates how starlight travels through its mirrors and reaches its detectors.

The team used powerful computational tools to adjust millions of parameters in the model, accounting for subtle movements, optical distortions, and other imperfections. By repeatedly refining the simulation until it closely matched the real observations, FLIP could reproduce the unwanted starlight more accurately and subtract it from the image.

This visualization demonstrates the image processing method, called FLIP, as it subtracts starlight from a James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observation of star 51 Eridani A (51 Eri) in the F430M filter. Starlight subtraction proceeds with the iteration number shown in the lower left, eventually revealing the faint planet 51 Eri b at its expected location. Credit: Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez

articles.title: Tangled quantum whirlpools caught unraveling in an ultracold gas
articles.dek: When a cloud of atoms is cooled close to absolute zero, its atoms can merge into a Bose–Einstein condensate (BEC): an exotic fluid in which atoms across the whole cloud share…
paragraphs: When a cloud of atoms is cooled close to absolute zero, its atoms can merge into a Bose–Einstein condensate (BEC): an exotic fluid in which atoms across the whole cloud share a single quantum state. Current theories predict that as a disordered quantum gas settles into this ordered state, a tangle of tiny vortices should form and gradually unravel.

Through new experiments detailed in Physical Review Letters , a team led by Sebastian Morris at the University of Cambridge has caught this process in action for the first time. Using a novel imaging approach, they directly observed the decay of these vortices—confirming the theory of "Vinen turbulence."

In a BEC, quantum behavior that is normally confined to individual particles plays out on a macroscopic scale. Like other quantum fluids, a BEC can't circulate freely like water: instead, any rotation is concentrated into thin, thread-like vortices, each carrying a quantized circulation.

According to a theory named "Vinen turbulence," newly formed BECs will contain a chaotic tangle of these threads, which gradually untangles as it relaxes. So far, physicists have seen hints of this effect in superfluid helium , but only indirectly. In atomic gases, vortices have mostly been imaged in flat, 2D systems. To properly test the idea in a 3D gas, researchers needed to both see the vortices and count them.

In their study, Morris' team started with a BEC of potassium atoms, held in a uniform, cylinder-shaped trap of light, less than a tenth of a millimeter across. They first disturbed the gas to scramble its ordered state, then switched on interactions between the atoms and let the system relax.

At different moments during this relaxation, they released the gas, magnified it around 3. 5 times and photographed a thin slice of the enlarged cloud. In these images, vortices appeared as dark streaks where the threads passed through the slice.

By repeating the process many times, the team estimated the total length of vortex threads packed into each unit of the gas's volume. This allowed them to test the theoretical law describing how this quantity should shrink over time.

As the gas relaxed, the vortex density fell just as predicted by Vinen turbulence: denser tangles decayed faster, as neighboring vortices interacted with each other. Later on, the decay slowed, as the remaining vortices were lost at the trap's walls.

Remarkably, the decay didn't depend on how strongly the atoms interacted. Once the team had accounted for the difference in particle mass, its rate also closely matched measurements in superfluid helium, even though the two fluids are utterly different at the microscopic level. The vortices became clearly visible at around the same time as the atoms began to show a pattern of growing quantum coherence .

Together, the results offer direct confirmation of theoretical predictions of how BECs emerge from disorder. Ultimately, the team's findings mark an important step forward in understanding how these exotic fluids behave.

articles.title: Researchers Have Discovered That a 6,000-Year-Old Clue to Ireland’s Farming History Was Completely Wrong
articles.dek: Protein tests on ancient bones have removed evidence of farming’s influence in Ireland before 4000 BCE, reopening questions about when the island first encountered agriculture.
paragraphs: Protein tests on ancient bones have removed evidence of farming’s influence in Ireland before 4000 BCE, reopening questions about when the island first encountered agriculture.

For more than 30 years, the “Kerry Cow” helped shape a story about how farming reached Ireland. Bone fragments found on the coast of County Kerry appeared to show that domesticated cattle had arrived while the island’s inhabitants still lived by hunting and gathering. A new analysis has revealed that those supposed cattle were a bear and a wild boar.

The fragments were unearthed during excavations in the 1980s and 1990s at Ferriter’s Cove, a small bay on the Dingle Peninsula. Dated to the end of Ireland’s Mesolithic period, which lasted from 8000 to 4000 BCE, they were considered the earliest evidence of domesticated farm animals in either Ireland or Britain.

Their identification as cattle challenged existing theories about Ireland’s transition to farming, suggesting that its hunter-gatherers had established links with Neolithic farmers arriving from continental Europe before agriculture took hold on the island.

Researchers led by Dr. Martin Moucheron at University College Dublin (UCD) returned to the original archaeological material, now stored at University College Cork (UCC). Working with Drs. Benjamin Gearey, Barra Ó Donnabháin, and Margaret McCarthy at UCC, and Kate Kanne at UCD, the team sent the bones to the CNRS laboratory in Lille, France.

There, the fragments underwent analysis using ZooMS, a technique that identifies animals through proteins preserved in ancient bone collagen, a structural component of bone. The results identified bear and wild boar rather than the domesticated cattle on which the earlier interpretation depended.

Reported in the latest edition of PAST , the newsletter of the Prehistoric Society , the findings remove a major piece of evidence from debates about when and how communities in Ireland and Britain moved from hunting and gathering to farming. There is currently no archaeological evidence supporting the idea that domesticated cattle, and by extension early farming communities, had reached or influenced Ireland before 4000 BCE. Losing that evidence does not establish a new arrival date, but it changes the basis for reconstructing that transition.

“Ferriter’s Cove is an iconic archaeological site, originally excavated by the Late Professor Peter Woodman, Department of Archaeology, UCC; this new collaboration with colleagues at UCD marks an exciting new phase of research and these remarkable results are set to change our understanding of the earliest evidence for agriculture in Ireland,” said Gearey.

The work is part of a Research Ireland-funded postdoctoral project at UCD’s School of Archaeology, led by Moucheron under the mentorship of Professor Graeme Warren. The project is reexamining important Mesolithic archaeological sites using modern scientific techniques.
Warren added, “These exciting results show the real value in going back to key sites with new analytical techniques – which can change the stories we tell about our past”

“For at least four millennia hunting and gathering people lived on the island, and there is a common conception that they left little trace and that we know very little about them – unlike the megaliths of Neolithic farmers, who are portrayed in ways that feel very familiar in Ireland,” said Moucheron.
“But there is much we can understand about Mesolithic people just by going back to the sites and material we have, and by looking at them with new eyes and new techniques – and an open mind.”

Further analyses are underway to determine whether the bear remains belonged to brown bears or polar bears. The researchers hope this work will provide new insights into Ireland’s prehistoric bear populations before their extinction during the Bronze Age.
Reference: “No sacred cows: ZooMS identification of the Late Mesolithic bone assemblage at Ferriter’s Cove, Co. Kerry, Ireland” .

Global temperatures may continue to rise even after human CO₂ emissions stop. The temperature change that follows is known as the zero emissions commitment (ZEC), and it is often assumed to be close to zero. A study led by the Met Office Hadley Center, with co-authors from several institutions including the University of Liverpool, found that the temperature response depends on how much warming has already occurred.

The authors used the UK Earth System Model (UKESM1. 2) to simulate what happens when CO₂ emissions stop at different levels of warming. At the lower warming levels extending up to 2°C above preindustrial temperatures, global temperature stayed roughly stable. When increased emissions led to higher warming levels of 3°C to 5°C above preindustrial temperatures, the model showed a further 0. 4°C to 0. 6°C of warming 150 years later.

The authors explained this response in terms of an energy imbalance for the Earth that continues for decades and centuries after emissions cease, in which the Earth still absorbs more energy than it loses to space. At higher warming levels, this energy imbalance was larger, driving more continued warming after emissions ended, and the cooling effect of land and ocean absorbing CO₂ was weaker.

Dr. Laura Gibbs, the lead author of the study published in Nature Climate Change , said, "This response matters for carbon budgets, which estimate how much more CO₂ can be emitted while keeping global warming below a given level. The greater the warming level, the more likely there is to be continued warming after emissions cease." The results of this study come from experiments with one climate model, but the results highlight why ceasing CO₂ emissions at lower levels of warming matters.

Professor Ric Williams, a co-author on the study at the University of Liverpool, said, "The different warming levels that are reached when we cease emitting carbon make a difference by altering the climate state, which then affects whether there is continued warming."

articles.title: What Is Science, Really? Even Scientists Can’t Agree
articles.dek: Even scientists in the same specialty disagree about science’s purpose, a survey finds, raising concerns that AI could automate one narrow approach at others’ expense.
paragraphs: Even scientists in the same specialty disagree about science’s purpose, a survey finds, raising concerns that AI could automate one narrow approach at others’ expense.

Is science a search for objective truth, an exercise in creative problem-solving, or both? A study published in Royal Society Open Science found that scientists disagree about the meaning and purpose of science more than the general public does.

Study leader Marina Dubova, a former Santa Fe Institute postdoctoral researcher, is now an assistant professor of psychology at the University of California, Berkeley. Working with Princeton University researcher Qiawen E. Liu, she surveyed 91 scientists and 99 members of the public. Participants evaluated 18 historical descriptions of science, including science as detective work, a search for truth, and a mirror reflecting reality.

Scientists and the public generally agreed that science involves following curiosity and solving mysteries. The public tended to share an idealized picture of science as a reliable way to discover how the world works, placing less emphasis on creativity or uncertainty. That outlook could shape how people judge research and help explain their frustration when scientists cannot give firm answers or revise their conclusions as new evidence emerges.

The public’s views were closer to those of physicists and biologists than to those of researchers in psychology or the social sciences. One possible explanation, Dubova suggests, is that physics and biology feature more prominently in science education. More research is needed to test that connection.

Some scientists emphasized the search for objective truth, while others gave more weight to the judgment and creativity researchers bring to their work. They also disagreed about whether research follows established methods or requires improvisation. Few of the 18 descriptions received scientists’ full support, and they often had reservations even about ideas they generally agreed with.

“What was surprising to me was that there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield,” says Dubova. She suspects that researchers develop their approaches partly through experience, much as chefs develop different instincts about when to follow a recipe and when to improvise. Those differing conceptions of science could influence which discoveries researchers pursue.

That diversity also raises a question for efforts to automate scientific research. As researchers develop artificial intelligence systems capable of conducting science, whose understanding of the work will those systems embody? Dubova worries that automation could reinforce one narrow conception of science at the expense of other valuable approaches.

For Dubova, the study is an early step toward understanding how these outlooks shape research itself. “Don’t take the common understanding of science for granted,” she says. “Always ask. Always be curious about what someone has in mind.”

The research was supported by SFI’s Lou Schuyler Seed Grant Fund, established in 2022 to support exploratory research by early-career scientists. Dubova used the funding to compensate study participants, helping make the research possible.

“Is science a search for objective truth, an exercise in creative problem-solving, or both?”
It is both. The two forms are the realms of theoretical/basic science and applied science.

Asking lay people what they think ‘science’ is, is asking them to share their ignorance. That is why the 99 were more in agreement on science. I doubt that many of the 99 could even describe the Scientific Method. How can one expect the public to understand what science is if they can’t describe the methodology?

articles.title: Giant, prehistoric rodent fossils discovered in southern Thailand
articles.dek: An international team of paleontologists, including researchers from McGill University, has discovered "remarkably large" rodent fossils in the pit of a mine in southern…
paragraphs: An international team of paleontologists, including researchers from McGill University, has discovered "remarkably large" rodent fossils in the pit of a mine in southern Thailand. The finding, published in Scientific Reports , provides a new perspective on the early manifestation of rodent gigantism—the process by which animals evolve to become larger—demonstrating that the evolutionary history of large-bodied rodents is considerably older and more geographically widespread than previously recognized, the researchers said.

The new species, Yakamys sirindhornae, lived approximately 34 million years ago, during the mid-Paleogene period. The researchers discovered fossils of its teeth—specifically, the lower second molar and lower incisor—at the Bang Mark Pit of the Krabi lignite mine in Krabi Province.

"Today, the largest living rodent is the capybara, but very large rodents are not restricted to recent ecosystems," said Virginie Millien, study co-author and professor of biology at McGill University. "Giant rodents evolved repeatedly during the later history of the group, mostly in South America. This discovery suggests that Southeast Asia also played an important role in the early evolutionary history of large-bodied rodents."
The new genus name, Yakamys, combines the Thai word "yak," meaning giant, with the Greek "mys," meaning mouse or rat.
"The species name, sirindhornae, honors Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn, in recognition of her longstanding support for science and paleontological research in Thailand," Millien said.

The fossils were discovered as part of a collaborative research project on fossil mammals in Thailand's Krabi Basin. The project involves researchers from McGill University, the Department of Mineral Resources of Thailand and French research institutions, including CNRS and Université de Poitiers.

Using seven established approaches for calculating body mass from dental dimensions, the researchers estimate that the Yakamys weighed approximately 30 kilograms (66 pounds)—about twice the size of other known rodents from this era, such as the Hulgana.
"This is only a ballpark figure, as there is substantial uncertainty associated with fossil body-mass estimation," Millien said.

Because the fossil material is limited, the researchers also noted that it is difficult to determine exactly how the Yakamys evolved. Further discoveries will be important for understanding the animal's biology, ecology and evolutionary history, they said.

articles.title: Prostate cancer testing now urged for men in their 50s and 60s – a lead author of the new screening guidelines explains why
articles.dek: The American Cancer Society announced on Nov. 12, 2026, that it has released major changes to its prostate cancer screening guidelines to improve detection and treatment of…
paragraphs: The American Cancer Society announced on Nov. 12, 2026, that it has released major changes to its prostate cancer screening guidelines to improve detection and treatment of the disease.
The Conversation asked Dr. Andrew Wolf , a physician at the University of Virginia who was one of the lead authors of the new guidelines , to walk readers through the changes and why they were made.

The biggest change is that we are making a proactive recommendation to screen for prostate cancer . Previously, we recommended that people talk with their healthcare provider to decide whether or not screening is right for them.
Our new recommendations vary by age and by a person’s risk of developing prostate cancer.

For people at average risk of developing prostate cancer, we recommend they be screened with the prostate-specific antigen, or PSA, blood test every two years from age 50 through 69. PSA is a protein that prostate cells make. Cancer and other conditions can cause PSA levels to rise.

People at higher risk, including Black men and men with a strong family history of prostate cancer, should be screened annually from age 45 to 69. A strong family history means having a family member who was diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65, or multiple family members diagnosed at any age. People with a single family member diagnosed at age 65 or older should be screened every two years from age 45 years to age 69 years.

For people ages 70 to 74, we recommend they talk with their healthcare provider about whether or not to continue screening. Because there is uncertainty about the benefit of screening for people in this age group, decision-making around screening depends on their personal preferences, overall health status and life expectancy.

For those over age 74, we recommend against prostate cancer screening. The potential harms of screening, such as more invasive follow-up tests and treatment, are likely to exceed the benefits for people in this age group.

Finally, we recommend against using a digital rectal exam to screen for prostate cancer, as it is less effective than the PSA test . The digital rectal exam may still be helpful when further evaluating elevated PSA levels or symptoms related to the prostate gland.
The past decade has seen mounting evidence supporting the benefits of using the PSA blood test to screen for prostate cancer.
The ability of the PSA test to reduce the risk of death from prostate cancer or of being diagnosed with metastatic disease are actually greater than researchers previously thought.

At the same time, there have been significant developments to reduce the potential harms associated with prostate cancer screening, including false positive PSA test results and diagnosis and treatment of prostate tumors that are unlikely to harm patients in the long-term.

Black men have an approximately two-thirds higher risk of developing prostate cancer compared with white men. They are also at greater risk for having more advanced disease at the time of diagnosis. These disparities are likely due to a combination of genetic, environmental, social and healthcare access factors .
Men with a family history of prostate cancer in a close relative – such as a parent, sibling or child – are also at elevated risk.

There are also a number of genetic mutations, such as BRCA2 , that confer significantly elevated risk of prostate cancer. Though screening recommendations for these cases are beyond the scope of our guideline, several professional medical organizations, including the National Comprehensive Cancer Network and the American Urological Association , have issued recommendations for screening people with these high-risk mutations.

For years, clinicians believed that the benefits of PSA screening were uncertain and didn’t necessarily outweigh the potential harms. This stance was in part because of the results of two large prostate cancer screening trials that were published in 2009. One, a U. S. study , found no benefit to screening; the other, a European study , found only a relatively small benefit.

However, it later became clear that the U. S. study was seriously flawed in such a way that it couldn’t have shown a benefit: Almost 90% of the men in the control group – that is, the group that wasn’t supposed to get screened – actually did get screened, and many of the men with abnormal PSA levels didn’t follow-up.

Conversely, most of the men in the European study who were randomized to standard care – no testing – instead of screening did not, in fact, get a PSA test, so it was more of a true comparison of the effect of screening versus not screening.

After researchers followed patients for over two decades in the European study, the effects of screening became clear: Screening reduced the risk of dying from prostate cancer by 13%. And about 500 men needed to be screened to avert one death from prostate cancer.

This may not sound very impressive, but it’s comparable to other routinely offered cancer screening tests, such as mammography for breast cancer . And the proportion of people needing to be screened to save a life would be significantly lower if extrapolated to a lifetime of screening starting at age 45 or 50, rather than the average number of two screenings that men received in the study.

The U. S. Preventive Services Task Force also has its own prostate cancer screening guidelines. The task force’s guidelines currently recommend that clinicians not screen for prostate cancer unless the patient indicates a preference to proceed. At the time of the task force’s last update in 2018 , it determined that the potential benefits and harms of screening were too closely balanced to recommend screening.
The task force has been in the process of updating those guidelines over the past several years. It is possible that their update will more closely align with that of the American Cancer Society.

I do think we have both sufficient evidence of benefit and sufficient reduction of the risks to now proactively recommend screening. Where the two guidelines do align is that both recommend that patients be informed of the benefits, risks and limitations of prostate cancer screening so they know what they’re getting into.

It is likely that our new screening recommendations will be covered by most insurers. However, patients may have out-of-pocket costs for further testing their doctor orders as a result of an abnormal PSA level.

articles.title: National ground stop response highlights critical errors in public reassurance – saying ‘nothing nefarious’ did the opposite of quelling public concern
articles.dek: Thousands of travelers were stranded on Nov. 13, 2026, when the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all domestic flights in the U.
paragraphs: Thousands of travelers were stranded on Nov. 13, 2026, when the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all domestic flights in the U. S. because of what they said were failures in decades-old air traffic communications systems . Crisis communications expert Shannon A. Bowen , a scholar at the University of South Carolina’s College of Information and Communications, spoke with The Conversation’s Politics and Legal Affairs Editor, Naomi Schalit, about how the Trump administration handled the first day of the crisis.

The first principle would be to react quickly and react with accuracy, react with everything you know at the moment, truthfully, but always react quickly. Because if you delay until you gather information, a vacuum will ensue. Information fills that vacuum that may not be accurate. And so that’s the enemy of accurate crisis communication, but you want to always speak quickly and be the most authoritative and definitive source, even if very little information is known.

A crisis unfolded and to the administration’s credit, they did react very quickly , in a way that offered the information that was known at the time, even though not a lot was known about why the ground stop was issued until later.
You’re speaking about the short press conference that afternoon with Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin?

He did keep saying that nothing nefarious was at hand . And for a crisis communication scholar, you would not want to introduce the idea that something nefarious was at hand, unless, indeed, something nefarious was at hand. So by the very act of introducing this concept and this idea, I think the talking point, “Nothing nefarious,” then went across multiple networks, and it became the center of a controversy rather than quelling a controversy.

By saying nothing nefarious is at hand, that indeed confirmed something nefarious was at hand, even if the nefariousness was only the mismanagement of the air traffic control systems routers that they claimed caused the problem. By introducing this idea, I believe it did bring to mind that there may be other state actors behind whatever happened, that it could be a cyber attack. It would have been better to say, “We have evidence that this was not a cyber attack but a hardware failure.”
How did the later press conference with Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy go from your perspective as an expert on crisis communications?
They handled the questions that they received correctly. They told us as much information as they knew.
However, they did seem to downplay the extent of this crisis, because we have to remember the traveling public is not just people trying to get to business meetings.

We had football teams stranded. Now football Saturday , all over the SEC, has been disrupted. And there’s probably disruption in other areas of the country, but to us in the South, SEC football is almost a religious experience on Saturday . Luckily, the University of South Carolina football team had already flown out . But our marching band was stuck in this crisis, and so we have a lot of ripple effects from something like this happening, and it definitely says to me that this was an emergency situation. It wasn’t simply a crisis, it was an actual emergency of impending disaster-level scale.

If it were simply routers being overloaded, as we’ve been told, why wouldn’t they already know this situation and restart those routers the night before or over Friday night after most of the traveling public is out of the air?
What was Mullin’s and Duffy’s job when they got out there? What did they need to do?

To inform the public about the danger, why this happened, the extent of the problem, and what they’re doing to remediate the problem. We keep hearing that they’re asking for US$30 billion and more to repair the whole infrastructure for the air traffic control system, which is great, but what are they doing right now?

How do we know that flights in the air, right this minute, are any safer than the ones yesterday, a minute before the ground stop? Do we have that information? I don’t feel confident that they addressed that question appropriately. I don’t think that the traveling public entirely feels safe at this point or adequately informed that they will arrive at their destination.
They introduced politics into the press conference as well, didn’t they?

It’s something that they have the prerogative to do. They are both political appointees and members of the cabinet . So I understand that aspect, but I really wish they had addressed the traveling public’s concerns more overtly before making it political, that they need more money to fix this. We know they need more money to fix it, and I’m sure the American taxpayers are aware of the problem and willing to fund those corrections. But the more expedient issues would be, what about all these people who were stuck in airports ?

I believe there were. We had another ground stop about three years ago , due to air traffic control problems, and that is what we call in crisis communications a “prodrome ,” a warning sign of larger impending problems. When you see these types of warning signs, it really gives us a reason to think it’s going to get worse.

Duffy did say on Nov. 13 that, because of the condition of the air traffic infrastructure, “ you will have more ” ground stoppages. If you had a piece of advice for the administration regarding their future communications, what would you tell them?

I would say to communicate in advance as much as possible, so if you’re even considering a ground stop, it may be a good idea to put out a public notice so that people don’t go to the airport on a vacation flight, maybe they delay that for a week or two. It might also be a good idea to speak with the airline industry representatives and say, “Here’s what we’re thinking. Can you work with us? How can we make this better for the traveling public?” Also, if 17 of 22 routers were malfunctioning, could we have had a partial ground stop at only the affected airports, rather than a nationwide stop?
My silly last question: Do crisis communications experts have any theories about Friday the 13th?

We consider it more of a superstition, but I have noticed that there does tend to be a lot of activity on Friday the 13th. It might be placebo effect, it might be because we expect something bad to happen and we’re looking for it. But that day does seem to always have some type of activity. This is also when organizations release bad news, oftentimes, they say, “Let’s hold it until Friday the 13th, because bad news is expected.” People will assume, on Friday the 13th, that negative things are going to come out, so the shock value won’t be as much.

articles.title: Why the Microsoft 365 outage is different and why it takes so long to restore email services
articles.dek: The Microsoft services outage that began on Nov. 12, 2026, is not like other internet outages.
paragraphs: The Microsoft services outage that began on Nov. 12, 2026, is not like other internet outages. The failure affected the Microsoft 365 suite of productivity services, including the video conferencing and collaboration platform Teams, AI assistant Copilot and, significantly, the Outlook email service.

Microsoft reported on Nov. 13 that the company is “continuing to see improvements in service availability” but that “some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery.”

Despite decades of predictions about its decline , email remains a central pillar of how organizations function. Password resets, invoices, legal notices and cybersecurity incident response coordination all depend on it. The Microsoft 365 outage affected businesses, governments and schools around the world.

When most people think about cloud outages , they picture a broken website or a stalled app. When the service going down includes email, however, the mechanics of the failure and how to recover from it are different from those of almost every other cloud service.
Unlike modern web apps or authentication gatekeepers, email wasn’t designed to fail fast, meaning to immediately halt when a problem arises.

When a typical cloud service breaks , it acts like a closed door. If an authentication provider or a cloud application goes down, users are immediately locked out and see an error message. Access stops. When people cannot get into the system, they are not actively generating new work or adding heavy processing loads to the broken servers. Once engineers fix the underlying bug and unlock the door, traffic can resume and the service often recovers fairly quickly.
Email does not have a closed door. It is built on an older, decentralized “store-and-forward” architecture designed to never lose a message, even when the destination is unreachable.

Because email is a network of thousands of independent systems, an outage at one major provider does not stop users on other platforms from hitting “send.” During major email disruptions like the one that hit Microsoft, millions of outside users on Gmail, corporate servers or other platforms could still compose and send emails to affected accounts without seeing an immediate error message.

From the sender’s perspective, everything works normally. Their email provider accepts the message, attempts to hand it off to the downed provider, realizes the destination isn’t answering, and quietly holds onto the message in an outbound queue to try again later.

One way to think about email traffic in outages is to imagine a multilane interstate highway where an accident blocks two lanes of traffic. Drivers miles away don’t stop leaving their driveways just because there is a wreck up ahead; they keep entering the highway system. Soon, traffic backs up so severely that metered on-ramps have to stop letting new cars merge onto the interstate. Before long, that gridlock spills backward onto local feeder roads and city streets, choking traffic miles away from the actual crash site.

In this analogy, a downed email provider is the crash. Every other email server around the world is an on-ramp or a feeder road. While the outage lasts, millions of messages continue to pile up in queues across the internet, with unaffected servers repeatedly resending email to see whether traffic is moving yet.

When engineers finally fix the root cause of an email outage, it is the equivalent of tow trucks clearing the wreckage from the highway. The road is technically open again, but traffic does not instantly return to normal speed.

First, the massive backlog of vehicles already stuck on the main highway has to start moving. Only after that congestion clears can the on-ramps start letting queued-up cars merge back in, which in turn slowly relieves the gridlock on the surrounding local roads.

Similarly, when a major email provider comes back online, it is immediately hit with a tidal wave of pent-up messages and retry attempts from every other mail server on the internet. Processing those queues without overwhelming the newly restored servers takes time – typically hours to days.

Because organizations have largely outsourced their email to a small number of global providers, an outage doesn’t just disrupt one company; it can stall entire sectors at once, cutting off the communication tool teams rely on to coordinate their emergency response.

And for everyday users, this unique architecture explains why email failures feel so drawn out: Even hours after a provider officially announces a problem is fixed, messages can still arrive out of order or trickle in slowly as the digital traffic jam finally clears.

articles.title: Oceans and forests have absorbed roughly half our carbon emissions for decades, slowing climate change – but can they keep it up?
articles.dek: Over the past two centuries, humans have pumped billions of tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere by burning fossil fuels , raising global temperatures in the process.
paragraphs: Over the past two centuries, humans have pumped billions of tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere by burning fossil fuels , raising global temperatures in the process.
Luckily for humanity, Earth has done what it could to soften the impact.
The world’s oceans have absorbed 35% of carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels since 1990, our new research shows, and the forests and other plants of the world have absorbed another 13%.

The importance of these two enormous natural carbon sinks cannot be overstated as global temperatures rise, fueling heat waves, fires, storms, floods and droughts around the world. Yet there is much that scientists do not understand about these carbon sinks – most importantly, how exactly they’ll behave in the future.

If the oceans and forests keep absorbing the same amount of carbon dioxide, scientists will have a sense of what to expect in the future and what can be done to slow climate change. And governments will know their remaining carbon budgets – that is, how much carbon dioxide can still be emitted into the atmosphere while keeping global temperatures below agreed-to levels.

We have been working on greenhouse gas measurements for decades. In a new study, published Nov. 12, 2026, in the journal Science, we describe an alternative method for measuring these crucial carbon sinks, and what it shows.

We found that while the ocean sink has been expanding, meaning the oceans are taking in more carbon dioxide, that expansion might begin to slow down , leaving the oceans less effective at absorbing carbon in the coming decades. We found that the land sink has not been expanding, which was something of a surprise.
Measuring how much carbon is being taken up by the world’s oceans and forests is devilishly difficult and prohibitively expensive.

This is because many parts of the land and ocean don’t behave in the same ways. What occurs in one ocean region or forest can be very different from another; and the behavior in one year can be very different in the next, often for reasons scientists do not fully understand.

Computer models can help overcome some of these complexities, but they too have limitations. Satellites can also help, but they cannot see through clouds, nor can they see what is happening in the soil or mid-to-deep ocean.
As carbon cycle scientists, we set out to find a different way to measure these carbon sinks.

Our new study approaches the problem from another angle. We used high-precision measurements of atmospheric oxygen (O₂), combined with atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) measurements , to quantify how the ocean and land carbon sinks takeing up carbon dioxide.

This works because land, oceans and burning fossil fuels have different effects on oxygen: When fossil fuels are burned, they not only produce CO₂, they consume O₂. On land, when plants take up CO₂ to grow, they simultaneously release O₂. When the oceans take up atmospheric CO₂, there is no corresponding release of O₂.

This means that if we measure both CO₂ and O₂ in the atmosphere, then we can quantify the ocean and land carbon sinks. It is a straightforward mathematical approach of solving two equations with two unknowns, combined with our knowledge and measurements of the global budgets of CO₂ and O₂.
When we looked at the ocean and land carbon sinks over the past three decades, the results were surprising and sobering.

In contrast to most computer model simulations , we did not find the land carbon sink increasing over time to keep pace with increasing fossil fuel emissions. We did, however, find a larger ocean carbon sink than predicted by most models , and we found that it has been increasing as emissions grow.

If these trends in carbon sinks continue, then in the coming decades, humans will be relying more heavily on the oceans to slow down climate change. But in the next few decades, there are reasons to believe the oceans could become less effective at absorbing carbon.

For example, warmer waters are not able to hold as much gas , such as carbon dioxide. Warmer surface waters are also less efficient at mixing into the deep ocean , which has the beneficial effect of locking carbon dioxide away from the atmosphere for many hundreds of years.
The data for the past decade hints at the possibility that while the ocean carbon sink is increasing now, its rate of increase may be slowing down.

For the oceans, most computer models agree with each other, but, for the historical period, they do not match our oxygen-based results. For the land, models vary widely from each other, and most do not match our oxygen-based results.

Computer models are essential to provide governments with feasible scenarios to avoid dangerous climate change, but to be effective they need to be better grounded in what real-world observations are showing. Nature is difficult to represent with a series of equations, and observations are few considering the size of the planet.

We believe our study improves understanding of global carbon sinks and can help lead to more reliable projections of what might happen with climate change in the coming decades. But like any scientific approach, our oxygen method also has drawbacks.

The measurements themselves are challenging, such that only about 10 research laboratories in the world are routinely doing them. Calibrating the measurements is an ongoing challenge. Earth is not helping: Warmer waters hold less gas, meaning that as oceans warm in response to climate change, they expel some oxygen into the atmosphere . We must account for this in our carbon sink calculations. And to take into account variability in ocean circulation and other ocean processes, we have to average our results over 10-year time frames.

Policymakers and the public need answers faster . We believe the solution involves both improving the atmospheric oxygen approach and using other independent approaches: measurements of carbon and oxygen in the oceans, computer models and satellites are all essential. Combining these approaches will lead to more robust understanding of the carbon cycle and climate change, and better knowledge of where these valuable carbon sinks and the global climate are headed.

articles.title: Gemini Astronaut Photos Inspired Early Earth Observation Program
articles.dek: Astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. orbited Earth from November 11 to 15, 1966, on Gemini XII , the final mission of NASA’s Gemini program.
paragraphs: Astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. orbited Earth from November 11 to 15, 1966, on Gemini XII , the final mission of NASA’s Gemini program.

In addition to successfully completing rendezvous maneuvers and spacewalks, procedures vital to sending American astronauts to the Moon, the crew was also spurring the development of a different field of exploration, observing Earth from space.

The photos taken by Lovell, Aldrin, and other Gemini astronauts demonstrated the value of orbital imagery for studying Earth’s surface. Their images helped scientists make the case for a dedicated Earth observation satellite program. One of strongest advocates for accelerating the use of Earth-observing satellites was William T. Pecora, the director of the United States Geological Survey from 1965 to 1971. articles.title: To get Americans to care about climate change, just call it climate change
articles.dek: You may be hearing phrases like “climate crisis,” “climate emergency” and “climate justice” a lot as the 2026 United Nations climate summit is underway.
paragraphs: You may be hearing phrases like “climate crisis,” “climate emergency” and “climate justice” a lot as the 2026 United Nations climate summit is underway. Political leaders, including U. N. Secretary-General António Guterres , are using them to try to get across the urgent risks and consequences of climate change. The danger is real , but is using this language actually persuasive?

It turns out that Americans are more familiar with – and more concerned about – climate change and global warming than they are about climate crisis, climate emergency or climate justice, according to a survey we conducted with a nationally representative sample of 5,137 Americans.
Moreover, we found no evidence that the alternative terms increased people’s sense of urgency, willingness to support climate-friendly policies or willingness to act.

The familiar terms – climate change and global warming – did at least as well, and sometimes better, than climate crisis and climate emergency in eliciting concern, perceived urgency and willingness to act. The phrase climate justice consistently tended to do worse, likely in part because it was the least familiar. These response patterns were similar among Republicans, Democrats and independents.
In our work as research psychologists , we have explored how Americans respond to the ways climate change is communicated and have uncovered a need to use straightforward language.

For example, people we interviewed for a study published in 2021 felt that climate experts were talking over their heads with terms like “adaptation,” “mitigation,” “sustainability” and “carbon-dioxide removal.” They wanted experts to use more familiar terms instead.

This inspired us to write a quick guide to climate jargon , published in The Conversation. Using everyday language makes information easier to understand, and even highly educated people tend to prefer it.

Jargon like “ biodiversity loss ” has similar problems. That refers to the shrinking variety of life on Earth, which is exacerbated by climate change. A survey of 7,338 U. S. adults led by one of us found people were much more familiar with and more concerned about “extinction of plants and animals” – or, if an explanation was provided, “nature loss”.

Even with an explanation, “biodiversity loss” was the least familiar and of least concern for people among several terms. Most people didn’t find “biodiversity crisis” or “extinction crisis” familiar either.
Yet, experts often use complex jargon because it is familiar to them, and they may not realize it is unfamiliar to others.

It has become common to talk about climate change and global warming as if they have the same meaning, but there are differences . Climate change refers to changes in the overall climate, while global warming refers specifically to rising temperatures.

A historical review found that, in the past, people were less likely to associate the term climate change with the idea that humans are actively warming the planet than they were with the term global warming. Perhaps this is why Democrats used to like the term global warming, while the popularization of the term climate change has been credited to Frank Luntz , an adviser to the George W. Bush administration.

Past surveys also found that Democrats used to think of global warming as being more serious than climate change, while Republicans thought of climate change as more serious than global warming. But according to a recent review , these partisan differences have now faded.

Alternative terms such as climate crisis, climate emergency and climate justice have been used to emphasize other aspects of climate change and to try to raise concern. In 2019, the British newspaper The Guardian switched to using climate crisis and climate emergency because it wanted to convey urgency.

Activists use the term climate justice to draw attention to climate change as a human rights challenge: Low-income people around the world suffer the most from the effects of climate change, despite being the least responsible for causing it.
Right now, the terms climate crisis, climate emergency or climate justice are less familiar and elicit less concern than climate change or global warming.

Even if these terms become more commonplace, there is no guarantee that they will heighten concern or inspire action. In fact, studies have suggested that phrases like climate crisis could backfire if they don’t resonate with people.

Our advice: Don’t make the mistake of using overheated language. Just stick with familiar terms that people understand – use global warming when referring to rising temperatures and climate change for overall changes in the climate.
This updates an article originally published Aug. 12, 2024 , with a new study and discussions at the 2026 U. N. climate conference, COP31.
